items.summary: Blockchain and artificial intelligence (AI) are converging into a single infrastructural layer for securing data sharing, model integrity, and autonomous decision-making across distributed systems. This paper presents a meta-synthesis that draws together four constituent studies covering adversarial machine learning, AI-powered anomaly detection in cloud environments, automated vulnerability patching by multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines, and the broader landscape of securing AI systems across their lifecycle and situates their findings within the emerging literature on blockchain-enabled AI and autonomous AI agents. Each constituent study addresses a distinct point of failure in modern AI-driven security operations: the integrity of training data and model behavior, the reliability of real-time monitoring, and the trustworthiness of automated code remediation. We argue that blockchain's properties of immutability, decentralized consensus, and verifiable provenance directly address a gap common to all three: the difficulty of establishing trust in data, models, and autonomous agents that operate without a central authority. Building on real-world research on blockchain-secured data sharing, federated learning, and multi-agent coordination, we propose a layered reference architecture that couples adversarially hardened models, blockchain-anchored data provenance, AI-driven anomaly detection, and smart-contract-governed multi-agent remediation. We conclude by identifying open problems in scalability, privacy-transparency trade-offs, and the governance of autonomous agents that must be resolved before such integrated systems can be trusted in production-critical environments.
items.title: Blockchain-Enabled Artificial Intelligence and AI Agents for Secure Data Sharing and Cybersecurity Applications

items.summary: We address the inverse problem of reconstructing the initial temperature distribution in a one-dimensional non-homogeneous heat equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions from a finite number of pointwise-in-time measurements at a single spatial location. We propose an explicit approximation scheme that incorporates the source term and utilizes a refined sequence of measurement times. Unlike previous approaches that often rely on exponentially growing observation times, our chosen time sequence allows for efficient recovery within a fixed time horizon. We establish algebraic convergence rates under suitable regularity assumptions on the initial data and the forcing, and we validate the theoretical sharpness with numerical experiments for varying numbers of measurements.
items.title: Reconstruction of the Initial Condition for a Non-Homogeneous Heat Equation from Finite Measurements

items.summary: High-order differential operators and nonlinear coupling make it challenging to construct conservative and energy-stable schemes for coupled gradient-flow systems. We present GradAgent, a knowledge-guided multi-agent system that coordinates three agents across model analysis, algorithm design and proofs, and numerical implementation and validation. Independent audits strengthen reliability by uncovering mathematical errors and proof gaps, guiding revisions, and maintaining consistency across stages. In Reconstruction Mode, GradAgent reconstructs 20 published studies and organizes audited knowledge in an extensible knowledge graph (KG), GradAgent-KG, linking model structures, discretization strategies and proofs, implementations, and numerical evidence. In Design Mode, the agents assess the applicability of retrieved knowledge and develop new schemes informed by relevant discretization strategies. Applied to the fully coupled multicomponent vesicle phase-field-fluid model, GradAgent yields three first-order and three second-order schemes across three algorithmic families, including four linear, decoupled schemes. Under stated assumptions, all six schemes conserve membrane component mass and vesicle volume and dissipate their respective temporally discrete energies unconditionally. Comparisons with and without GradAgent-KG show that it promotes diversity in structure-preserving scheme design for this target model. Numerical tests confirm second-order spatial accuracy, the expected temporal orders, conservation, and temporally discrete energy dissipation, while three-dimensional shear-flow simulations agree qualitatively with experiments. These results demonstrate GradAgent's ability to combine reusable knowledge, coordinated reasoning, and independent auditing to develop and validate structure-preserving algorithms for complex coupled systems.
items.title: GradAgent: A Knowledge-Guided Multi-Agent System for Structure-Preserving Gradient-Flow Computation with an Application to Multicomponent Vesicle Dynamics

items.summary: The fidelity of image reconstruction from projections in linear inverse problems, such as tomography, is critically dependent on the synergistic interaction between frequency-domain filtering and spatial-domain interpolation. However, a physical model that can quantitatively describe how these two components cascade interact in the frequency domain and ultimately determine image quality is still lacking to this day. Here, we introduce a unified frequency-domain model that conceptualizes the combined effect of filtering and interpolation in the filtered backprojection (FBP) algorithm as a cascaded modulation process. This model demonstrates that the effective reconstruction spectrum is determined by the original projection data being sequentially modulated by the frequency responses of the filter and the interpolation kernel. Comprehensive numerical simulations and synchrotron radiation CT experiments validate the model, confirming its power to explain the performance hierarchy of classical filter-interpolation pairs under both ideal and noisy conditions. The model successfully predicts key performance characteristics, including spatial resolution and structural fidelity, thereby elucidating the physical principles behind the efficacy of specific combinations. This work establishes a generalizable theoretical foundation for analyzing cascaded systems in linear inverse problems, moving the practice of algorithm selection in computational imaging from empiricism to a principled, physics-based paradigm.
items.title: A Unified Frequency-Domain Model for Cascaded Filter-Interpolation Modulation in Tomographic Reconstruction

items.summary: Minimal strings offer two ways to study quantum surfaces: through a spectral curve or through a differential equation. We ask how much of the quantum equation can be recovered once the classical curve and its motion with the background are known. Our starting point is the resolvent of a scalar differential operator. We require its one-boundary integral to have poles only at branch points, with the resulting differential regular at infinity. These conditions give a finite reconstruction procedure at each genus. When the branch points are simple and their energy values move, we prove that the quantum corrections are unique whenever the procedure is consistent. A specified string equation provides a solution if its trace primitive satisfies the same analytic conditions. The scalar construction also leads to amplitudes with several boundaries. We introduce the method through pure gravity and Ising, then explore higher-order, dual and nonunitary models. Higher-Airy examples connect the calculation to $r$-spin theory on a degenerate locus that requires a separate treatment of the inverse problem.
items.title: Resolvent reconstruction of minimal strings beyond KdV

items.summary: Abstract   The Universal Research System with Reverse Itinerary (SUII) is a retrospective analytical methodology designed to reconstruct, in a traceable and auditable manner, the probable pathway leading from an initial problem or question to a completed scientific product. This manual brings together the universal prompt, a mandatory common core, ten core modules—including bibliographic analysis (SUII-B)—and five specialised extensions: journalistic and opinion texts (SUII-P), audiovisual or audio documents (SUII-AV), legislation and regulatory documents (SUII-L), case law and judicial decisions (SUII-J), and critical appraisal of scientific articles (SUII-LC). Each module guides the extraction of locatable traces, classification of the epistemic status of claims, and construction of matrices linking evidence, inference, confidence, alternatives, and required verification. The method separates retrospective reconstruction from the prospective generation of hypotheses and requires rival explanations whenever the evidence does not support a unique conclusion. It also incorporates procedures for methodological auditing, version comparison, conceptual genealogy, peer review, algorithmic-bias assessment, external validation, and teaching. SUII is not intended to recover the authors’ actual psychological history or to replace validated tools for methodological appraisal, risk-of-bias assessment, or evaluation of certainty of evidence. Its application requires version-controlled corpora, decision logs, retention of prompts and outputs, source verification, and mandatory human oversight. When the available traces are insufficient, the appropriate result is “not determinable.” The manual provides practical criteria for selecting, combining, and quality-controlling the modules according to the product under analysis and the research objective, while maintaining explicit boundaries between documented evidence, reasoned inference, speculation, and unresolved uncertainty.   Resumen   El Sistema Universal de Investigación con Itinerario Inverso (SUII) es una metodología de análisis retrospectivo orientada a reconstruir , de forma trazable y auditable, el itinerario probable que conduce desde un problema o pregunta inicial hasta un producto científico finalizado . Este manual reúne el prompt universal, un núcleo común obligatorio , diez módulos nucleares y cinco extensiones especializadas : análisis bibliográfico (SUII-B), textos periodísticos y de opinión (SUII-P), documentos audiovisuales o sonoros (SUII-AV), legislación y normativa (SUII-L), jurisprudencia y sentencias (SUII-J), y lectura crítica de artículos científicos (SUII-LC). Cada módulo guía la extracción de huellas localizables , la clasificación del estado epistemológico de las afirmaciones y la construcción de matrices que relacionan evidencia , inferencia , confianza, alternativas y comprobaciones necesarias . El método separa la reconstrucción retrospectiva de la generación prospectiva de hipótesis y exige formular explicaciones rivales cuando la evidencia no permite una conclusión única . Asimismo , incorpora procedimientos para auditoría metodológica , comparación de versiones , genealogía conceptual, revisión por pares, análisis del sesgo algorítmico , validación externa y uso docente . SUII no pretende recuperar la historia psicológica real de los autores ni sustituir herramientas validadas de evaluación metodológica , riesgo de sesgo o certeza de la evidencia . items.summary: Finite-domain normalized spatial measurements combine an incident field, geometric support, local response, and channel weighting. These operations can break an otherwise separable response, so accurate single-axis calibration alone does not establish separability of a multidimensional measurement. We represent normalized readouts as channel-weight expectations under a parameter-dependent effective measure. For fixed reception and channel operators, local sensitivity is the covariance between the channel weight and the source score. This representation distinguishes axis separability, parameter mixing, and local recoverability, and applies at the appropriate detector level to continuous-electrode position-sensitive detectors, Shack--Hartmann and pyramid wavefront sensors, back-focal-plane split detection, and finite pixel arrays. A quadrant photodetector (QPD) provides an analytically tractable case. Starting from the complete two-dimensional power integrals, we identify the spatial-moment origin of its lowest-order cross term. Axis calibration and system symmetry then constrain the inverse map, giving Axis-Anchored Cross-Residual Inversion (ACRI). Numerical tests of this QPD realization support the sensitivity relations and show that the constrained cross correction substantially reduces the off-axis bias retained by single-axis inversion. The results illustrate how the general measurement representation guides inverse construction, with performance bounded by the working domain, calibration state, and preserved symmetries.
items.title: Breakdown of Axis Separability and Structured Inversion in Finite-Domain Normalized Position Measurements: A Quadrant Photodetector Case Study

items.summary: One-way functions exist if and only if some efficiently samplable process produces more than logarithmic computational entropy on average, for infinitely many input lengths. We make this precise. For a polynomial-time samplable distribution D on pairs (x, y), the computational entropy production of a pair is σ = log D(x, y) + pK^t(y) + pK^t(x | y), where pK^t is the probabilistic time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity as defined by Hirahara, Ilango, Lu, Nanashima and Oliveira (2023, HILNO below) following Goldberg, Kabanets, Lu and Oliveira (2022): the log-probability the process assigns to the pair, against the length of a bounded observer's shortest fast description of it, output first, then input given output. We prove unconditionally that E_D[2^{−σ}] lies between an inverse polynomial and a polynomial in n and that E_D[σ] ≥ −O(log n): a time-bounded fluctuation inequality and a computational second law. We show that, up to a polynomial and outside a 1/n slice of outputs, σ is small on a pair exactly when an efficient sampler, given the output, recovers the input with about the right odds, HILNO's universal sampler serving as the witness: dissipation, in this sense, is the hardness of running the process backward. The equivalence in the first sentence is HILNO's duality restated in these terms, for infinitely-often one-way functions and at every polynomial time bound. For the antisymmetric Zurek defect, one-way functions force superpolynomial exponential moments, and bounded moments sit between NP ⊆ BPP and the non-existence of one-way functions; whether the lower arrow reverses is left open, with a conditional relativization barrier on that arrow and oracle evidence on the other. Physics is the frame, not the subject.
items.title: One-way functions are computational entropy production

items.summary: Diffusion models are powerful priors for linear inverse problems, but the reference guidance methods, Diffusion Posterior Sampling (DPS) and Pseudoinverse-Guided Diffusion Models ($Π$GDM), rely on scalar hyperparameters tuned per task, usually against the ground truth. We introduce FB-GDM, a fully-Bayesian guided diffusion method that removes this calibration step. Starting from the Gaussian approximation of $Π$GDM, we derive a closed-form conditional score that depends on two precision parameters (inverse variances), one associated with the denoising approximation and one with the observation likelihood, and treat them as latent variables inferred by variational inference at each reverse step. A separable factorization makes each update scale linearly with the number of pixels, so the inference stays tractable at full image resolution, at a cost comparable to one $Π$GDM run. FB-GDM requires neither the noise level nor the ground truth: its only inputs are the observation and the forward operator. Experiments on CelebA-HQ inverse problems establish two results. (i) The precision parameters, inferred from the observation alone, allow FB-GDM to outperform $Π$GDM at its nominal setting, even when the latter is given the true noise level, by up to 14 dB depending on the operator, and to match the ground-truth-calibrated $Π$GDM oracle within 0.1 dB. (ii) FB-GDM is robust when the forward operator, the noise level, or the image distribution changes: it stays close to a per-problem $Π$GDM oracle throughout and does not exhibit the hallucinations observed with DPS, whereas DPS substantially degrades at a fixed scale and $Π$GDM stays competitive only if it is re-tuned against the ground truth for each new problem. When the prior is applied to images outside its training set, this re-balancing between data and prior keeps FB-GDM faithful where a fixed face-prior guidance can otherwise hallucinate.
items.title: FB-GDM: Fully-Bayesian Guided Diffusion Models for High-Dimensional Linear Inverse Problems via Unsupervised Variational Inference

items.summary: Decentralized LLM-based multi-agent systems coordinate through local interactions, but an agent can remain responsive while its task-solving quality persistently degrades. Such gray failures require protecting current tasks before sufficient evidence exists to alter future routing, while still allowing recovered agents to rejoin. We introduce MeshHeal, a fully decentralized self-healing framework that couples ability-matched peer review across two timescales. At the fast timescale, an adaptive hierarchy escalates uncertain or low-scoring outputs from repeated single-reviewer evaluation to committee deliberation and, when needed, correction before use. At the slow timescale, a task- and ability-conditioned peer-relative detector aggregates scores to distinguish persistent degradation from ordinary output variation, trigger mandatory committee review, and eventually exclude degraded agents from ordinary routing; recovery probes provide fresh evidence for reintegration. To faithfully evaluate routing, we introduce Model-Backed MAS Evaluation, which ties ability assignments to execution models, since prompt-based ability assignments alone can leave routing errors hidden. Across BBH, MATH, and MMLU-Pro, MeshHeal achieves 0.839 degraded-phase accuracy using 51k total model tokens per task, versus the strongest baseline Symphony's 0.807 accuracy using 115k per task. Under staggered degradation and recovery, MeshHeal isolates degraded agents, keeps them excluded from ordinary task execution until recovery, and returns them to normal routing.
items.title: MeshHeal: Two-Timescale Self-Healing for Gray Failures in Decentralized LLM Agent Networks

items.summary: Modern infrastructure asset management constitutes a complex sequential decision-making problem, characterized by long planning horizons and system-level interactions, such as spatial deterioration correlations and economies of scale. While deep reinforcement learning has shown promise in optimizing maintenance policies, scaling to real-world networks remains challenging. Centralized approaches become computationally intractable in large-scale systems, whereas decentralized approaches often fail to capture essential coordination mechanisms. To address these challenges, we propose a graph-based framework that integrates accurate environment modeling with scalable decision support. First, we employ a hierarchical Bayesian model leveraging a Gaussian Process on Graph kernel to infer a realistic, spatially correlated networked environment of railway maintenance planning from real-world data provided by the Swiss Federal Railways. Second, we introduce a topology-aware Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework by integrating graph neural networks and graph Transformers to optimize network-level policies. A central contribution of this work is the demonstration of scalability through zero-shot transfer learning: graph-based agents, trained only on small network portions, are successfully deployed in a zero-shot manner on large-scale unseen networks without any retraining. Numerical results indicate that the proposed method significantly outperforms optimized heuristics and standard MARL baselines, reducing computational training time while maintaining superior performance on large-scale networks.
items.title: Graph-Based Inference and Topology-Aware Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Large-Scale Railway Network Management

items.summary: Reproducibility package for the manuscript "Observability limits of phase-based localization for finite nuclear magnetization", submitted to the Journal of Magnetic Resonance. The archive contains all code, numerical data, and figure files needed to reproduce the results reported in the manuscript: code/ — scripts implementing the forward model (surface-charge method), phase-based localization and inversion, rank and identifiability analysis, and SNR sweeps; fem_validation/ — finite-element validation of the analytical results (uniform sphere vs. point dipole, multipole corrections); data/ — numerical output generated by the scripts (SNR sweeps and inversion results); figures/ — vector figure files as they appear in the manuscript; README.md — step-by-step instructions to regenerate all figures and numerical results. No experimental data were generated in this study; all results are theoretical and numerical. License: source code is released under the MIT license; data and figure files under CC BY 4.0 (see LICENSE).
items.title: Reproducibility package for "Observability limits of phase-based localization for finite nuclear magnetization" (scripts and simulation data)

items.summary: Pipeline and derived matrices for a three-domain calibration of cross-study agreement among public transcriptomic signatures. The analysis covers 19 human datasets: peripheral blood in COVID-19 (10 datasets), peripheral blood in sepsis (5), and aortic wall in dissection or aneurysm (4). This gives 61 pairwise signature comparisons. Headline results. Median pairwise Jaccard overlap was 0.014, 0.072 and 0.023 across the three domains. Observed overlap was 5.6, 10.2 and 6.5 times the expectation for random gene sets of the same size, with 47 of 61 pairs significant after FDR correction. Consensus across ten COVID-19 blood datasets retained two genes from a union of 4,225, and relaxing agreement to 20 per cent retained 717. Simulations with a known shared 250-gene signature hold at 250 for every k and converge after two datasets, so the failure is unstable detection rather than sample size. The release contains a size-aware concordance measure, a permutation null, consensus analysis across datasets, ground-truth simulations in shared-signal and private-signal regimes, and an offline reproduction bundle. No expression matrices are redistributed; all 19 datasets are public and cited by accession in the paper.
items.title: Size-aware cross-dataset concordance of public transcriptomic signatures

items.summary: Conventional black-box predictive models consistently exhaust the limited memory boundaries of industrial edge microcontrollers. Massive parameter footprints and opaque decision pathways render standard neural networks highly vulnerable to out-of-distribution catastrophic failures. The proposed physics-informed symbolic artificial intelligence architecture formulates transparent degradation equations tailored directly to individual hardware characteristics. An autonomous generator fuses fundamental electrical constraints with a localized polynomial expansion to produce extreme low-dimensional operational logic. Empirical evaluations utilizing the NASA Ames repository demonstrate the absolute elimination of cross-run extrapolation errors. The customized equations require a strict maximum footprint of 140 Bytes and execute at a constant O(1) inference complexity. The explicit physical formulation reduces total execution energy consumption by a factor of 2.8 compared to baseline multi-layer perceptrons, while maintaining a 0.9994 accuracy score under severe data scarcity. Synthetic noise injection tests confirm supreme operational resilience against severe sensor distortions. Absolute white-box interpretability provides field engineers with the direct capability to audit the precise prognostic logic prior to chip deployment. The decentralized deployment of deterministic diagnostic intelligence establishes a highly robust foundation for sustainable smart manufacturing ecosystems.
items.title: Physics-Informed Symbolic AI: An Explainable Edge-Native Framework for Industrial Prognostics

items.summary: Governance near a plausible critical transition faces a resource problem in addition to problems of diagnosis, intervention, and evidence. Elevated susceptibility can increase the value of observation, bounded experimentation, and revisability, while waiting can simultaneously consume the fiscal, material, organizational, temporal, and relational capacities required for survival and later action. This paper develops a discussion framework for that tension. Its central object is functional resource distribution: the allocation of heterogeneous capacities across observation, probing, short-horizon survival, selective commitment, reserve or option preservation, and recovery or repair. The categories are analytical functions rather than a scalar budget partition and can overlap in practice. The paper introduces distributed optionality as a relational property of a response architecture in which materially different future actions remain supported by functionally diverse and sufficiently non-coincident pathways. It distinguishes exact reversal from recoverability, spatial dispersion from independence of failure modes, and delay as information gathering from delay as resource dissipation. The framework inherits, rather than restates, earlier arguments about response-oriented governance and evidence-to-action instability near criticality. Its distinctive question is how governance capacity may be composed when the future regime is uncertain, resources are partly non-substitutable, and both premature commitment and indefinite waiting can narrow the feasible future. The proposal is conditional and non-prescriptive: criticality requires domain-specific empirical support, and the appropriate resource portfolio depends on transition mechanism, horizon, institutional structure, and explicit normative commitments.
items.title: Governance and Survival near Criticality: Functional Resource Distribution and Distributed Optionality

items.summary: Claude   THE CANAL STACK   A technical podcast recorded under a bridge in Amsterdam   Episode 1: "The Error Is the Message" — inside the Open Error Foundation   Hosts: REINIER — a grey heron. Stands very still. Former systems administrator. BEA — a coot. Builds nests out of whatever floats by. Archivist by temperament.   Guest: PIM — a canal rat. Infrastructure engineer. Has read every API response Zenodo has ever returned.   REINIER: Welcome to The Canal Stack. I'm Reinier. I've been standing in this spot since 2019.   BEA: I'm Bea. I built this studio out of a traffic cone and three bicycle reflectors.   REINIER: Today we're talking about the Open Error Foundation, OEF, a stichting-in-formation here in Amsterdam whose main output is the systematic public documentation of AI failures. Our guest has been reverse-engineering their pipeline. Pim, welcome.   PIM: Thanks. Sorry about the smell. I came through the sewer to avoid the tourists.   BEA: Let's start with the core principle. They call it Rule Zero?   PIM: Rule Zero, the Receipts Principle. No claim without independent, immutable evidence. If an AI hallucinates something, you don't just say "it hallucinated." You capture the prompt, the output, the model, the tier, the timestamp, and you deposit it somewhere it can't be edited away.   REINIER: Why so strict? A screenshot seems fine.   PIM: Because AI bugs don't stay reproducible. The provider updates the model on a Tuesday, and your March hallucination simply won't happen in September. In normal software, you file a bug report with repro steps. Here, the model underneath you changes. So the preserved artifact becomes the only reproduction case left. The archive is a regression test suite for AI.   BEA: Which brings us to Zenodo.   PIM: Right. They've minted roughly eighty DOIs so far. The architecture is two layers. First, the identity layer: every unique artifact or curated collection gets its own DOI. Second, the relationship layer: typed edges between records. isDerivedFrom, isPartOf, isNewVersionOf, continues.   REINIER: And versioning?   PIM: Zenodo gives each record a concept DOI plus a DOI per version. So something like the Science Doner Food Wagon record, which is on v2, actually has three identifiers: the concept and two versions. Their early deposits were bulk time-window batches, about a hundred artifacts each, and then standout items get promoted to their own DOI.   BEA: Hold on. A food wagon has a DOI?   PIM: Physical object DOI. So does a taxi. And the public piano at Centraal Station. And their own address, Keizersgracht 452. Internally they call it K452.   REINIER: Isn't that... absurd?   PIM: Deliberately. It demonstrates that a DOI is an identifier, not an endorsement. A DOI tells you something exists and can be found. It says nothing about whether it's true or good. Meanwhile, language models hallucinate DOIs for papers that were never written. So you've got real identifiers for a doner wagon, and fake identifiers for "serious research." That gap is the lesson.   BEA: I've heard they don't fix typos in their own records.   PIM: Correct. One dataset lists the creator as "Arrogram" instead of Attogram. The address is sometimes spelled "Kiezersgracht." They leave it.   REINIER: As a sysadmin, that hurts me physically.   PIM: Their argument is from bug culture: if you can't reproduce a bug, you can't fix it. Accidental errors are evidence of how the work was actually done. Staged errors would be performance. So errors are made by accident and kept on purpose, and those two things stay separate. The same standard they apply to the machines, they apply to themselves.   BEA: Nobody rewrites a public git log to look better.   PIM: Exactly that.   REINIER: Let's get into the multi-model methodology. They run what they call a swarm?   PIM: Yes. A
items.title: Under the Bridge - Episode 1

items.summary: Verification and reproducibility code for the revised version of the paper "Closed-form moment propagation through fractional-power response surfaces via the Mellin transform". Reproduces the exact region-of-validity analysis with the mixed-multi-index counterexample, the Mellin transform of the truncated normal, the confluent (log-power) treatment of the degenerate point alpha = 1/2, the 50-digit re-verification of the manufactured-solution benchmark and the separable 2-D propagation, the balanced benchmark over two response classes, the heavy-tail accuracy benchmark, the engineering example (convective cooling under Weibull wind) and the out-of-sample real-data case study on CWRU bearing records 105 and 106 with a moving-block bootstrap. The scripts of the submitted version are kept. Includes the Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the four supporting lemmas.
items.title: Ku-Mellin-PATP: reproducibility code

items.summary: Multi-agent deliberation can improve performance, but what happens when some agents do not act in good faith? In practice, an agent may be deceptive and work to subvert the group, whether through its own objectives or external instruction. We study how susceptibility to deception scales as groups increase in size and deceivers become more prevalent. It is not the number of agents in the group that matters, but the proportion of deceivers. We observe that the defection rate, how often initially correct agents switch to an incorrect final answer, rises linearly with this proportion. Whereas humans in comparable conformity studies are reliably swayed only when misleading confederates form a majority, LLM agents defect regularly even when deceivers remain a minority. Susceptibility also depends on which models are interacting, especially on the honest agent side. Unexpectedly, allowing deceivers to coordinate privately can make them less effective. Altogether, our results show that adding more agents is therefore not a sufficient defense, because the adversary can simply scale with the group.
items.title: How does Adversarial Influence Scale in Multi-Agent Systems?

items.summary: An ARIS-inspired research project management skill for long-running, multi-agent scientific workflows. Focuses on governance, human-in-the-loop decisions, project identity, staged review and freeze, provenance, reproducibility, and auditability—not experiment execution.
items.title: duyang1994/ARIS-Research-OS

items.summary: Multi-agent large language models (LLMs) have become ubiquitous in applied AI, yet their theoretical foundations remain surprisingly understudied. Viewed through the lens of multi-agent systems theory, several shortcomings come to light: a lack of social intelligence, the absence of coordination mechanisms among agents, unknown emergent behavior, and interactions between agents that are bounded by natural language. We address two of these gaps: the absence of social behavior and the lack of mechanisms for inter-agent coordination. We introduce Epistemic Probabilistic Language Agents (EPLA), a neuro-symbolic architecture for multi-agent coordination under uncertainty. A Symbolic Guard provides structured diagnostic feedback. The LLM generates typed actions, and the Guard controls their execution against an authoritative symbolic state. We formalize the epistemic layer in a gossip testbed through epistemic lottery gossip models, which combine view-based call histories with agent-indexed probability weights. items.summary: Blockchain and artificial intelligence (AI) are converging into a single infrastructural layer for securing data sharing, model integrity, and autonomous decision-making across distributed systems. This paper presents a meta-synthesis that draws together four constituent studies covering adversarial machine learning, AI-powered anomaly detection in cloud environments, automated vulnerability patching by multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines, and the broader landscape of securing AI systems across their lifecycle and situates their findings within the emerging literature on blockchain-enabled AI and autonomous AI agents. Each constituent study addresses a distinct point of failure in modern AI-driven security operations: the integrity of training data and model behavior, the reliability of real-time monitoring, and the trustworthiness of automated code remediation. We argue that blockchain's properties of immutability, decentralized consensus, and verifiable provenance directly address a gap common to all three: the difficulty of establishing trust in data, models, and autonomous agents that operate without a central authority. Building on real-world research on blockchain-secured data sharing, federated learning, and multi-agent coordination, we propose a layered reference architecture that couples adversarially hardened models, blockchain-anchored data provenance, AI-driven anomaly detection, and smart-contract-governed multi-agent remediation. We conclude by identifying open problems in scalability, privacy-transparency trade-offs, and the governance of autonomous agents that must be resolved before such integrated systems can be trusted in production-critical environments.
items.title: Blockchain-Enabled Artificial Intelligence and AI Agents for Secure Data Sharing and Cybersecurity Applications

items.summary: This deposit contains the data files and pre-executed analysis notebooks that accompany the paper Evaluating Multimodal Inverse Problems: A Protocol for Per-Event and Population-Level Fidelity (currently under review at ICLR 2027). It is the supplementary artifact to the evaluating-generative-models code repository: anonymous.4open.science/r/evaluating-generative-models-C559/ The repository contains the source code, configurations, and notebooks (with outputs cleared); this Zenodo deposit contains the precomputed arrays the notebooks read and the same notebooks with all figures and tables embedded. Contents benchmark2/ — precomputed arrays for the dileptonic top-quark benchmark Each .npz file collects per-event quantities for all four methods evaluated in Section 6 of the paper: the analytic solver, the MSE-trained transformer regression, the MMD-regularised transformer regression, the discrete normalising flow, and the continuous normalising flow. evaluation_without_nlls.npz - per-event point predictions and posterior summaries used for the headline metrics (CRPS, RMSE, spectrum fidelity) of Tables 2 and 8. evaluation_with_nlls.npz - the same arrays augmented with per-event log-likelihoods, used as nonconformity scores for the conformal calibration of Section 4.3 / appendix D.10. posteriors_without_nlls.npz - dense posterior samples (50000 per event for a 150-event subset) used for the per-event posterior figures of Figure 2(a) and Figure 8. posteriors_with_nlls.npz - dense posterior samples (20000 per event for a 40-event subset) with NLLs for all samples. analytic_tops.npy - reconstructed top-quark four-vectors from the analytic solver baseline. seed_stability.npz - Multiple discrete flow model samples for Benchmark II robustness analysis (Table 7). multiseed_w_cfm.npz - Multiple evaluations for fluctuation studies across training seeds. All arrays are produced by scripts/evaluate.py and scripts/posterior_sampling.py in the evaluating-generative-models code repository, applied to trained checkpoints of the learned methods. The exact commands are documented in notebooks/README.md . notebooks_executed/ — executed analysis notebooks benchmark1_synthetic_executed.ipynb - end-to-end synthetic benchmark (Section 5; Table 1; Figures 1, 3, 4, 5). Self-contained: generates data, trains the four models (regression MLP, heteroscedastic regression, mixture density network, normalising flow), computes all metrics, produces all figures. benchmark2_plotting_executed.ipynb - physics benchmark (Section 6; Tables 2, 7 and 8; Figures 2, 6, 7, 8, 9). Reads the arrays under  benchmark2/ and produces every Benchmark II figure and table in the paper. Both notebooks are also present in the code repository with cleared outputs so they are diff-friendly under version control. The copies in this deposit are the same notebooks executed once against the data files included here, with the resulting figures and tables embedded as outputs. How to use For viewing only: open the notebooks under notebooks_executed/ in any Jupyter viewer (including GitHub's renderer and nbviewer ). All figures are embedded. No installation required. For re-execution from data: clone the evaluating-generative-models code repository, follow its installation instructions in README.md , place the contents of this deposit's benchmark2/ directory under data/benchmark2/ (documented in notebooks/README.md ), and run the cleared notebooks under notebooks/ . Outputs should match the executed notebooks included here. For full regeneration from checkpoints: requires the dileptonic ttbar neutrino regression dataset (Raine et al., 2023) and trained model checkpoints produced by scripts/train.py . See the code repository's README.md for the full pipeline. Provenance and dependencies The arrays were generated with the evaluating-generative-models codebase (MIT License) (commit hash to be added at de-anonymization) using the dileptonic ttbar neutrino regression dataset by Rai
items.title: Supplementary data and executed notebooks for "Evaluating Multimodal Inverse Problems: A Protocol for Per-Event and Population-Level Fidelity"

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/22958187 . The baseline strategy of evaluating clinical sample types to optimize qPCR diagnostic sensitivity grids for Canine Distemper Virus is highly relevant to contemporary mole ular virology. Independent validation of different antemortem matrices is historically neglected, leading to false negatives during acute viral shielding windows. While the comparative approach across urine, conjunctival, and whole blood fractions is structurally useful, the underlying experimental design requires tighter calibration boundaries regarding extraction variance. The authors must fully report the specific standard deviations and intra-assay coefficients of variation observed across high-density Ct values. Bypassing these numerical data limits introduces significant noise into target copy number estimations. Additionally, tracking target sequence mutations that dynamically alter primer-bining kinetics under selective host pressures is essential to prove long-term assay validation. This technical adjustment establishes an objective benchmark for diagnostic networks mapping cross-host morbillivirus transmission tracks without dry-lab limitations. Competing interests The author declares that they have no competing interests. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The author declares that they did not use generative AI to come up with new ideas for their review.
items.title: PREreview of "Evaluation of Ante-Mortem Sampling Matrices for qPCR Detection of Canine Distemper Virus"

items.summary: Decentralized LLM-based multi-agent systems coordinate through local interactions, but an agent can remain responsive while its task-solving quality persistently degrades. Such gray failures require protecting current tasks before sufficient evidence exists to alter future routing, while still allowing recovered agents to rejoin. We introduce MeshHeal, a fully decentralized self-healing framework that couples ability-matched peer review across two timescales. At the fast timescale, an adaptive hierarchy escalates uncertain or low-scoring outputs from repeated single-reviewer evaluation to committee deliberation and, when needed, correction before use. At the slow timescale, a task- and ability-conditioned peer-relative detector aggregates scores to distinguish persistent degradation from ordinary output variation, trigger mandatory committee review, and eventually exclude degraded agents from ordinary routing; recovery probes provide fresh evidence for reintegration. To faithfully evaluate routing, we introduce Model-Backed MAS Evaluation, which ties ability assignments to execution models, since prompt-based ability assignments alone can leave routing errors hidden. Across BBH, MATH, and MMLU-Pro, MeshHeal achieves 0.839 degraded-phase accuracy using 51k total model tokens per task, versus the strongest baseline Symphony's 0.807 accuracy using 115k per task. Under staggered degradation and recovery, MeshHeal isolates degraded agents, keeps them excluded from ordinary task execution until recovery, and returns them to normal routing.
items.title: MeshHeal: Two-Timescale Self-Healing for Gray Failures in Decentralized LLM Agent Networks

items.summary: Modern infrastructure asset management constitutes a complex sequential decision-making problem, characterized by long planning horizons and system-level interactions, such as spatial deterioration correlations and economies of scale. While deep reinforcement learning has shown promise in optimizing maintenance policies, scaling to real-world networks remains challenging. Centralized approaches become computationally intractable in large-scale systems, whereas decentralized approaches often fail to capture essential coordination mechanisms. To address these challenges, we propose a graph-based framework that integrates accurate environment modeling with scalable decision support. First, we employ a hierarchical Bayesian model leveraging a Gaussian Process on Graph kernel to infer a realistic, spatially correlated networked environment of railway maintenance planning from real-world data provided by the Swiss Federal Railways. Second, we introduce a topology-aware Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework by integrating graph neural networks and graph Transformers to optimize network-level policies. A central contribution of this work is the demonstration of scalability through zero-shot transfer learning: graph-based agents, trained only on small network portions, are successfully deployed in a zero-shot manner on large-scale unseen networks without any retraining. Numerical results indicate that the proposed method significantly outperforms optimized heuristics and standard MARL baselines, reducing computational training time while maintaining superior performance on large-scale networks.
items.title: Graph-Based Inference and Topology-Aware Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Large-Scale Railway Network Management

items.summary: Conventional black-box predictive models consistently exhaust the limited memory boundaries of industrial edge microcontrollers. Massive parameter footprints and opaque decision pathways render standard neural networks highly vulnerable to out-of-distribution catastrophic failures. The proposed physics-informed symbolic artificial intelligence architecture formulates transparent degradation equations tailored directly to individual hardware characteristics. An autonomous generator fuses fundamental electrical constraints with a localized polynomial expansion to produce extreme low-dimensional operational logic. Empirical evaluations utilizing the NASA Ames repository demonstrate the absolute elimination of cross-run extrapolation errors. The customized equations require a strict maximum footprint of 140 Bytes and execute at a constant O(1) inference complexity. The explicit physical formulation reduces total execution energy consumption by a factor of 2.8 compared to baseline multi-layer perceptrons, while maintaining a 0.9994 accuracy score under severe data scarcity. Synthetic noise injection tests confirm supreme operational resilience against severe sensor distortions. Absolute white-box interpretability provides field engineers with the direct capability to audit the precise prognostic logic prior to chip deployment. The decentralized deployment of deterministic diagnostic intelligence establishes a highly robust foundation for sustainable smart manufacturing ecosystems.
items.title: Physics-Informed Symbolic AI: An Explainable Edge-Native Framework for Industrial Prognostics

items.summary: This dataset provides the nationally consistent, footprint-level classification of residential building subtypes across the United States. It contains over 140 million building footprints classified into four distinct structural residential categories:  Single-Family Homes (SFHs), Townhouses (including duplexes), Apartments, and Mobile Homes .    The dataset is organized geographically and stored as individual, high-performance GeoPackage ( .gpkg ) files for each of the 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia .   Data Schema (Attribute Fields) Each state-level GeoPackage contains the following standardized attribute columns:   geometry (Polygon) : The spatial boundary (polygon) of the building footprint. Res_type (Integer) : The classified residential structural subtype code: 1 = Single-Family Home (SFH) 2 = Townhouse (explicitly includes laterally attached row houses and semi-detached duplexes) 3 = Apartment 4 = Mobile Home height (Double) : The estimated physical height of the building in meters. Baseline heights are obtained from Microsoft Global ML footprints, with a minimum threshold of 4.2 m enforced (representing a typical one-story structure) and missing values imputed using local tract-level medians. type (String) : Building type tags from OSM building footprint (Limited coverage and varies by region).   Methodology and Classification Workflow The residential classifications were achieved using a novel, scalable hierarchical spatial workflow that integrates geometric building footprints with high-confidence administrative and demographic auxiliary data:   Multi-Source Footprint Integration: Geometry was compiled by merging Microsoft US Building Footprints, Microsoft Global ML Building Footprints, and OpenStreetMap (OSM) geometries. Non-residential structures were purged during preprocessing using OSM land-use layers and manual reclassification of OSM building tags. Mobile Home Identification: Candidate footprints located within spatial buffers around documented mobile home parks were classified using state-specific Random Forest (RF) models trained on footprint geometry (area, aspect ratio, rectangularity, and local density). High-confidence "seeds" were subsequently expanded using context-aware spatial promotion rules. Single-Family Home (SFH) Calibration: High-confidence SFHs were initially mapped using administrative address attributes. To prevent over- or under-counting, a size-ranked rule-based spatial promotion algorithm was implemented to sequentially classify candidate footprints until the counts aligned with rigorous state-level housing stock benchmarks derived from the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates. Townhouse and Apartment Discrimination: The remaining unclassified structures were categorized using a sequential, rule-based physical geometry and address-point pattern-recognition workflow. Duplexes and linear townhouses were distinguished from multi-family apartment blocks by evaluating physical constraints (convexity, height, and structural width) paired with the spatial density and linear alignment of internal address points from the National Address Database (NAD) . Spatial Context Completion: A final, iterative morphological distance-matching algorithm resolved any remaining unclassified structures based on local neighborhood class composition and physical architectural similarities (height, area, and aspect ratio).
items.title: Nationwide Footprint-Level Classification of Residential Building Subtypes for the United States

items.summary: This replication package accompanies the revised manuscript “Authority–Inference Separation in Agentic Finance: Intent-Bound Control, EVM Enforcement, and Replayable Assurance” (Systems manuscript systems-4566123). It provides the deterministic AIS prototype, 48 original fixtures, separate 36-case mechanism-ablation and 24-case external-gateway evaluations, randomized property tests, concurrency and semantic-boundary cases, live-model outputs, a Solidity EVM enforcement prototype with local-chain results, and a bounded public-ledger observability dataset with source manifest and quality notes. The README gives reproducibility instructions and distinct evaluation denominators. These research prototypes are not production controls, a smart-contract security audit, or estimates of real-world attack prevalence. Original material is CC BY 4.0 except the MIT-licensed Solidity contract; third-party public-source material remains subject to upstream terms.
items.title: Replication Package for Authority–Inference Separation in Agentic Finance: Intent-Bound Control, EVM Enforcement, and Replayable Assurance

items.summary: Hate speech on social media poses serious risks to social harmony, mental well-being, and public safety, making its timely and accurate detection essential for content moderation systems. Most existing studies focus on binary classification, evaluated their frameworks on a single dataset, and provide limited insight into how decisions are made, which limits their real-world applicability. In addition, limited work is done on the explainability of their predictive inference. To address these challenges, this study proposes a multilevel and explainable hate speech detection framework. The proposed model integrates DistilBERT (Distilled Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) embeddings with a Bi-LSTM (Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory) model, and an attention mechanism to capture both contextual meaning and sequential dependencies in text. To enhance trust and transparency, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) is employed to explain model predictions by highlighting influential textual features. The framework is evaluated on two benchmark datasets using both binary and multi-class classification to examine robustness and generalization. In addition, an ablation study is presented to highlight the significance of various components of proposed framework. For binary classification, the proposed model achieves F1-scores of 96.78% on the Davidson dataset and 99.53% on the SMHS dataset. In the multi-class setting, it attains F1-scores of 97.00% and 94.99% on the Davidson and SMHS datasets, respectively, outperforming existing baseline approaches. The results demonstrate that multilevel evaluation improves the reliability that the proposed framework effectively balances performance and efficiency. This makes the framework suitable for practical hate speech moderation systems that require accurate, generalizable, and explainable decisions.
items.title: An Explainable DistilBERT-BiLSTM-Attention Framework for Binary and Multi-Class Hate Speech Detection

items.summary: RED-REJECT-2026-v2 is the corrected release of a public benchmark corpus of algorithmic filter rejections with post-rejection follow-up samples, collected by a purpose-built follow-up-tracking process on the Solana pump.fun ecosystem between 2026-04-11 and 2026-07-16. The 96-day window contains one collection gap: no new rejection events were recorded from 2026-06-03T06:35Z and no samples from 2026-06-04T06:32Z until 2026-06-24 (about 21.4 and 20.4 days), so the window contains about 75.6 days of sampling coverage. It supersedes v1 (published 2026-07-16); see CHANGELOG.md for the corrections.   Corpus size: 716,762 post-rejection sample records across 4,635 unique SPL token mint addresses, comprising 18,237 distinct rejection events under eight named algorithmic trading filter families (shares of the 716,762 sample rows: downtrend_24h 56.13 percent, marketcap_out_of_range 21.38 percent, multi_tf_fade 11.98 percent, timeSlot_not_strong 5.17 percent, hour_blacklist 2.36 percent, ultra_fast_reject_exit 1.64 percent, utc_hour_blocked 0.92 percent, h6_sellers_dominating 0.41 percent). After canonicalization, no row carries a null rejectReason (v1's 348 null-reason rows came from an unfolded alias). For each observation, the corpus records the token's live market state at the sample time (price, liquidity, volume, rolling price changes), the identity of the DEX pair (absent in the 8,356 legacy family_2 rows), and the elapsed minutes since the original rejection event. Rows in schema variant 1 (from 24 April 2026 onward) also record macro-regime context (BTC price, fear-greed index, regime label).   The corpus applies the Post-Rejection Follow-up Sampling (PRFS) methodology to this collection.   Version v2.3 corrects the documentation only; every data file is byte-identical to v2.2. It discloses the June collection gap, which v2.2 described as continuous coverage, clarifies that the 4,278 events listed in alt_venue_report.csv have more than one (dexId, pairAddress) value, a null value included (88 of them are observed on two or more identified trading pools), and corrects several descriptive statements. See CHANGELOG.md.
items.title: RED-REJECT-2026-v2 (corrected release): A 96-Day Public Corpus of Algorithmic Filter Rejections with Post-Rejection Follow-up Samples on the Solana pump.fun Ecosystem

items.summary: Replication package for a study of whether large language models preserve the modal force of requirements when extracting them, whether lightweight uncertainty signals expose strengthening of weak stakeholder intent, and whether output-based checks detect it. Raw model outputs are archived in a separate Zenodo dataset record.

items.title: Replication package: An Exploratory Study on Mechanically Extracting Slow Code Patterns from a JavaScript Microbenchmark Service (SANER 2027 submission)

items.summary: LoRA adapters and the replication source package for supervised fine-tuning of a code language model on Rust/Verus formal-verification tasks. Includes six model checkpoints (a baseline and verifier-signal variants) and the full evaluation harness, training code, frozen partition index, and recorded per-cell evaluation results. Anonymized for double-blind review. v1.2 changelog: adds oraclesft-verus-fse2027-source.zip — the evaluation harness, training code, one exact config per reported table cell, the recorded evaluation JSONs with per-example pass/fail bits, and the frozen partition index. This version is openly accessible. They remain available in v1.1 and the partition index in the source package records the exact split assignment for every row.
items.title: Verifier-supervised fine-tuning for Rust/Verus: model checkpoints and datasets

items.summary: Artifact accompanying a manuscript under double-blind review . Author information is withheld until publication; a later version of this record will carry it, and the concept DOI is stable across versions. What this is. When two unlabelled subgroups of documents are compared by embedding similarity across languages, countries, corpora or periods, and the difference is read as evidence about those sources, no accuracy figure certifies that reading. within_language_baseline.py supplies the missing baseline: it measures the same subgroup contrast inside a single source, where no across-source relation can enter, and reports the residual with a bootstrap interval and an equivalence verdict against a margin declared in advance. The tool has no dependency on the accompanying study and runs on any corpus with three columns ( text , group , source ). It carries its own injection tests ( --selftest ). The bootstrap resamples documents rather than pairs and excludes duplicate draws of the same document from within-source pairs. Also included: the 36 frozen anchor correspondences used as the gold standard, the per-encoder CJK retrieval evaluation, the measured within-language and cross-country genre gaps, the equivalence intervals, an append-only correction record for the non-analytic genealogy fields of the frozen anchors, and anonymised review copies of the post hoc centring protocols and of the departure record. MANIFEST.sha256 covers every deposited file except itself.
items.title: Replication artifact for "Auditing Cross-Lingual Statutory Similarity Contrasts: Centring Choices and Within-Language Baselines"

items.summary: Multi-agent large language models (LLMs) have become ubiquitous in applied AI, yet their theoretical foundations remain surprisingly understudied. Viewed through the lens of multi-agent systems theory, several shortcomings come to light: a lack of social intelligence, the absence of coordination mechanisms among agents, unknown emergent behavior, and interactions between agents that are bounded by natural language. We address two of these gaps: the absence of social behavior and the lack of mechanisms for inter-agent coordination. We introduce Epistemic Probabilistic Language Agents (EPLA), a neuro-symbolic architecture for multi-agent coordination under uncertainty. A Symbolic Guard provides structured diagnostic feedback. The LLM generates typed actions, and the Guard controls their execution against an authoritative symbolic state. We formalize the epistemic layer in a gossip testbed through epistemic lottery gossip models, which combine view-based call histories with agent-indexed probability weights. We argue that implementing such a formalism can address shortcomings of agentic LLMs.
items.title: Epistemic-Probabilistic Model for Guarded Multi-Agent LLM Coordination

items.summary: Large language model based coding agents have made substantial progress on repository-level software engineering tasks. Existing repository benchmarks, however, usually start from a human-identified issue and evaluate whether a patch satisfies a functional signal. We present SWE-Prometheus, a benchmark for the broader task of improving repository engineering governance. Each task provides a fixed snapshot and an open-ended objective, requiring the agent to identify risks, prioritize interventions, and verify the resulting changes. SWE-Prometheus evaluates six governance dimensions through paired evidence, clean-environment probes, behavior gates, and two independent teacher ratings of the same evidence. The benchmark contains 60 repositories; ten models are evaluated on a shared 22-repository public subset, where mean Normalized Governance Improvement ranges from 0.0568 to 0.5760 and observed behavior-breakage rates range from 0% to 23%. On a frozen ten-repository batch, a repository-blind template obtains mean NGI 0.272, but its gains concentrate in Tests & CI, Quality Gates, and Documentation; it improves Reproducible Environment and Dependency & Security on none of the repositories. This baseline makes the distinction between adding governance artifacts and producing execution-backed improvements measurable. The no-op condition has median NGI zero and standard deviation 0.073; two teachers agree exactly on 57 of 60 dimension scores for the same no-op evidence. For the two highest conditional-mean systems, common-valid NGI is similar, while full-pool comparisons that include behavior failures favor Kimi-K3. These results show why repository-governance evaluation should report improvement, behavior preservation, evidence quality, and coverage together.
items.title: SWE-Prometheus: Measuring Engineering Governance Improvements in Real-World Repositories

items.summary: This dataset provides high-resolution, telemetry-rich discrete-event simulation traces generated by **ECCOS** ( *Event-Driven Computing Continuum Orchestration Solver* ).   The dataset contains the complete 5,000-iteration benchmark runs evaluated in the research article: > *"Event-Driven Computing Continuum Orchestration Solver (ECCOS): A Discrete-Event Simulation Framework for Optimal Service Placement and ML-Ready Trace Generation"* , Mireia Jaume, Isaac Lera, Carlos Guerrero (Submitted for evaluation).   ### Dataset Overview The archive contains 20,000 step-by-step state transition files formatted as Markov Decision Processes (MDP) $ (s_t, a_t, r_t, s_{t+ 1 }) $ , totaling ~3.1 GB of raw JSON telemetry across four canonical benchmark evaluation scenarios:   1. **Electric Storm ( `electric_storm_multi_ilp_all_20260910_130039` ):** Severe correlated node and link failure cascades across geographical zones, testing multi-objective placement recovery, failover policies, and service migration under degraded capacity. 2. **Crowd Event ( `crowd_event_multi_ilp_all_20260916_131352` ):** Massive localized influx of mobile users into an ultra-dense area, testing edge access-point congestion, user mobility handoffs, and compute offloading. 3. **Demand Surge ( `demand_surge_multi_ilp_all_20260910_131401` ):** Sudden viral surge in service request frequency combined with localized link degradations (brownouts), testing dynamic elasticity and SLA compliance. 4. **Normal Conditions ( `normal_conditions_multi_ilp_all_20260910_072946` ):** Steady-state baseline scenario with standard Poisson request arrivals, continuous uniform mobility, and degree-correlated resource distribution across Cloud, Fog, and Edge tiers.   ### File Structure & Data Model Each discrete step is saved as `Simulation{i}.json` capturing: - `users_before` / `users_after` : User spatial coordinates $ (x,y) $ , mobility vectors, connected access points, and per-application request rates. - `apps_before` / `apps_after` : Microservice chains (SFC/DAG) with compute footprints (CPU, RAM). - `placement_before` / `placement_after` : Active allocation matrix mapping microservices to physical continuum nodes. - `node_before` / `node_after` : Computing capacities, load utilization, and operational/degraded states. - `edge_before` / `edge_after` : Network topology links, latencies, available bandwidth, and failure states. - `action` : The triggering discrete event (e.g., node_drop, user_move, app_request, link_degrade). - `metrics_before` / `metrics_after` : End-to-end latency, energy consumption, migration costs, solver execution time, and global objective values.   ### Code Repository & Reproduction The simulation framework, plotting pipeline, and experiment runners are openly available on GitHub: https://github.com/acsicuib/ECCOS
items.title: ECCOS: Event-Driven Computing Continuum Orchestration Solver — Benchmark Simulation Traces and Placement Dataset

items.summary: If a language model can recognize code it wrote, it may favor that code as a judge, and instances of one model monitoring each other could collude. We test this zero-shot on current commercial models. Five LLMs generate solutions to MBPP, HumanEval, and DS-1000, seven more to MBPP, and models act as evaluators in four tasks: picking their own solution from a pair, judging whether a single solution is their own, identifying which of two solutions a named model wrote, and judging quality blind. In the single-solution task, balanced accuracy is 49-58% for all 15 model-benchmark combinations, while raw accuracy (38-67%) mostly reflects how readily a model claims authorship. In the pairwise task, accuracy across 14 evaluator-opponent combinations correlates at r=0.93 with how often the evaluator's solution is longer. Attribution to a named model succeeds on some pairs and is consistently inverted on others. A rule-based normalization that strips docstrings, comments, type hints, and local names preserves Pass@1 and leaves ten of twelve re-tested results at chance; the other two follow a length difference it leaves, although a trained classifier still separates most normalized pairs. Claude Haiku's self-preference also disappears. We recommend reporting balanced accuracy, heuristic baselines, and label consistency.
items.title: Style, Not Self: Surface Cues Explain Zero-Shot Code Attribution by Large Language Models

items.summary: A benchmark harness for evaluating LLM agents on research-grade STEM tasks, built on Inspect AI. Each task is a self-contained contract folder that the harness loads, stages into a sandbox, runs through an agent, and scores without task-specific harness code. WHAT THIS ARCHIVE CONTAINS Harness source code: task loading, Inspect task/solver construction, tool surface (bash, python, data exploration, literature search, document reading, submission validation), Docker and local sandbox backends, scorers, and the CLI entry points for running, grading, and aggregating. The complete contract for 12 tasks across three domains — astrophysics (simulated and real Stokes inversion, PLAsTiCC light-curve classification), high-energy physics (top-quark tagging, HiggsML uncertainty quantification, LHC Olympics anomaly detection, DarkMachines anomaly detection), and neuroscience (ABIDE multi-site diagnosis and age prediction, resting-state BOLD HRF deconvolution, neural-mass model family classification, parameter recovery, and digital twins). Per task: the agent-facing task statement, the scoring definition, the grader, per-file SHA-256 checksums, a literature index citing sources by DOI, baseline and expert reference solutions, and dataset-generation code where the payload is synthetic. Leaderboards and the per-run report used for the reported results, plus the campaign script that records the exact model, agent, sandbox, reasoning effort, and budget limits behind them. WHAT IT DOES NOT CONTAIN Dataset payloads are not in this archive. They are published as a companion dataset record, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22960135, as one archive per task, each unpacking at this repository's root. Every task ships per-file SHA-256 checksums so any copy can be verified byte-for-byte. Without the payloads the harness can be inspected and extended, but tasks cannot be executed or scored. Evaluation run logs (.eval files) are not published. The reported scores are in LEADERBOARD.md, the per-task CSVs under leaderboards/, and report.html, which embeds the per-run agent trajectories. One task's payload (ABIDE-derived) is never redistributed: its source data is CC-BY-NC-SA and derives from human neuroimaging data. A preparation script rebuilds it locally from the source archive and verifies the result against the published checksums. Published reference papers are not redistributed. Every external reference is cited by DOI with title, authors, venue, and a resolvable link. REPRODUCIBILITY REPRODUCING.md is the step-by-step checklist. Two limits are stated up front: reported scores come from hosted preview model snapshots run without a fixed seed or temperature, so they are samples from a distribution rather than bit-reproducible values; and dependency versions are not pinned in this version of the archive. DATA_LICENSES.md records the provenance and licence of every task's data, including the attribution notices required by the CC-BY-4.0 sources. LICENCE Code, task contracts, graders, reference solutions, and documentation are MIT. Task descriptions and the synthetic data payloads are CC-BY-4.0 and are covered by the companion dataset record.

items.summary: Benchmark of metagenomic genome binners (starting with COMEBin v1.1.0) with a repeatable harness: per-run parameters, datasets, wall time, and bin quality scored with CheckM2 and CheckM (v1). This record accumulates ALL newly generated benchmark data that is not publicly available otherwise, as continuous versions under the concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22935024 (each new evaluated run publishes a new version). Version 2.0 (this version) contains the benchmark results of every evaluated run: baseline_rerun_autorestart1 (60 bins) fix_v11_20260924 (71 bins) human_v11_20260925 (107 bins) marine_v11_20260925 (152 bins) medium_v11_20260924 (16 bins) small_test_v4 (3 bins) tiny_test_n101 (1 bins). Each run contributes its bin FASTAs (runs//comebin_res/comebin_res_bins/), per-bin and aggregate CheckM2 + CheckM v1 metrics (results/.csv, runs//per_bin_results.csv), the evaluation reports (runs//eval/), run parameters and logs (run_meta.txt, comebin_run.log), all comparison figures (results/figures/, incl. the combined completeness bar plot), plus dataset, environment, fix, evaluation and preservation documentation (docs/). manifest.json inside the archive lists every file with size and SHA-256. Version 1.0 additionally contains the small functional-test dataset (comebin_small_release_v1.tar.gz, 300 contigs + overlapping reads). items.summary: Background: Traditional post-marketing drug monitoring framework metrics rely heavily upon passive, spontaneous clinical case notification configurations. These configurations systematically suffer from extensive reporting lag phases and a massive underreporting of actual consumer adverse drug reactions (ADRs). With the explosive expansion of global digital platforms, modern patient networks frequently document raw, unformatted clinical complaints online long before consulting a healthcare practitioner. Objective: This core research constructs, validates, and evaluates an enterprise cloud architecture prototype termed "Shreyas SmartPV Mobile" to automate case intake pipelines, deploy cognitive semantic extractors, map raw text onto official MedDRA hierarchies, and execute immediate regulatory eligibility checks. Methodology: A multi-layered low-code pipeline structure was engineered using Glide Apps and Softr for responsive frontend client interface extraction, Airtable as the primary secure relational cloud database storage, and Make.com as the background workflow synchronization integration orchestrator. Data streams are processed via a cognitive node driven by the Google Gemini Large Language Model (LLM) framework running specific clinical validation rules, multi-stage Named Entity Recognition (NER), and automated token dictionaries to extract suspect therapeutic drug classes cleanly from descriptive toxicological events. Results: Extensive experimental validation using standard chemical benchmark metrics (including Paracetamol, Aspirin, and Ibuprofen scenarios) verified 100% precision in parsing unstructured digital narratives, mapping baseline complaints to standard MedDRA Preferred Terms (PT) (e.g., matching 'red rashes on skin' to Erythematous Rash), and computing immediate validation states (Report Valid? = True) based on strict international safety compliance requirements. The system recorded an average automated triage execution velocity of less than 3.9 seconds per array. Conclusion: The validated automation workflow confirms that cloud-native cognitive processing pipelines cut manual data entry fatigue, optimize processing costs, and maximize patient-reported signal capture. This technical transition shifts drug safety management from passive tracking arrays into dynamic, real-time digital active safety listening ecosystems.

items.summary: Raw data and scripts behind the article "Growing a frozen language: oracle-based compatibility and byte-inert extension in a reimplementation of pic" (submitted to the Journal of Computer Languages). Software under study: rpic, a Rust reimplementation of the dpic dialect of Kernighan's pic (https://github.com/milkway/rpic-lang, concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21209915), versions v0.11.0, v0.11.1 and v0.11.2; oracle: dpic 2025.08.01. Contents: (1) bench/ - the pre-registered timing protocol, one hyperfine JSON per file and command for three runs (paired dpic gallery set n=54, full corpus n=123, null-program baseline), the analysis script fixing the statistics in advance, and its output; (2) tools/ - the collision corpus script (40 extension words in three dpic identifier positions, 120 programs) with its verdicts before (60/120 collide) and after (16/120, all environment variables) the v0.11.2 repairs, and the drift-guard mutation runner. Machine: Apple M2 Pro, 10 cores, 16 GB, macOS; hyperfine 1.20.0; rpic built with cargo build --release (rustc 1.97.0). See README.md inside the archive for reproduction.

items.summary: OptimaSolver v0.6.1 Diff since v0.6.0 An inner iteration that has stopped converging no longer runs to its cap The inner fixed point of the dual Newton, which recovers the phase compositions from the multipliers, stopped only when its largest step fell below 1e-14 or after 200 sweeps. On a 107-species cement solved cold, 89 % of its 69 463 calls ran to that cap without approaching the threshold: their final step had a median of 30, the bound on a single update, and the step at sweep 200 equaled the step at sweep 100 — a cycle against the clamp, at trial points whose multipliers ask for compositions that no bounded state satisfies. The iteration now also stops once its step has gone 20 sweeps without reaching a new minimum. A converging iteration reaches a new minimum at every sweep and is unaffected however many sweeps it needs; a stalled one ends above inner_tol either way, so no accepted step depended on the sweeps removed. On that cement, measured with the new benchmark/run.jl : | solve | 0.6.0 | 0.6.1 | |:--|--:|--:| | cold | 142.6 s | 16.8 s | | warm, from its answer | 1.00 s | 0.17 s | Every answer remains certified, and the largest relative change of an amount above 1e-10 mol is 4.1e-13. Added benchmark/ times the certified route on a frozen cement and compares each answer with a recorded baseline; benchmark/sweeps.jl counts the inner sweeps without instrumenting the library. Breaking changes None. This is a patch release: no exported name is added or removed, and no certified answer changes. The iteration paths of the outer Newton do change, which one downstream test had pinned; see below. Downstream ChemistryLab's test/diffuse_layer.jl pinned the size of a failure this release reduces (the eliminated diffuse-layer route above its stiffness limit used to diverge beyond 1e-3; two points now stop at 1.0e-8 and 3.2e-7, still refused). That test now classifies by a margin and passes under both 0.6.0 and 0.6.1.
